title: How Convenience Stores Make Money
fullText: Ask somebody what a convenience store sells and you get two answers. Fuel and cigarettes. Both answers are correct. Both are also from the store side of the counter close to worthless. Fuel is 65% of what the American convenience industry sells. The industry turned over $817 billion last year. 476 billion of that was fuel. That fuel produced 38.8% 8% of the gross profit. 2/3 of the money going in, a third of the profit coming out. Cigarettes are worse. Inside the shop, they are the biggest line on the wall, or near enough, just under 19% of everything sold indoors. They generate 7% of the indoor gross profit. So, the two things the place is famous for are the two it barely earns on, which leaves a question. Something in that building is paying for the building. It is not what you would guess and in the end it is not really a product at all. Start at the pump. It is the biggest number and the most misunderstood one. There is a belief that fuel retailers gouge you. The sign changes twice a day. The price never falls as fast as it climbed. It feels like a con. Here is the actual arithmetic. Across last year, American fuel retailers made a gross margin of a bit over 40 cents on a gallon. That is the figure before anything comes off it. Then things come off it. Delivery, the tanks, the pumps, the canopy lights, the staff, the insurance. There is also the environmental compliance. You are storing a very large quantity of flammable liquid underneath a car park. Industry figures put the retailers take after all of that at 10 to 15 cents a gallon and that is before tax. 40 cents a gallon. Gross. Now guess what survives to the bottom. Do not look it up. Put a number in the comments in cents. Then keep watching because the answer arrives in about a minute. A lot of people are going to be a long way out. Like the video if your guess turns out too high. subscribe if it turns out too low. There is one more subtraction and it rarely gets counted. When you tap a card at the pump, the card networks take a cut. On fuel, that cut has been measured at around 8 12 cents a gallon. Read that against a 10 to 15 cent net. On great many transactions, the payment company earns more from the sale than the retailer does. The retailer bought the tanks. He dug the hole, hired the staff, and carries the liability. He still comes a second to the company that moved the money. And there is a reason the fuel price is so exposed. It is the only price in retail written in numbers a meter tall facing traffic legible at 40 mph. You can compare the four stations without leaving the car. So, nobody can charge more than the man across the road. The sign is not really a price. It is an advertisement priced at almost nothing pointing at a door. Now the wall behind the counter. Cigarettes have anchored this business for 50 years. In 2015, there were 30.9% of everything sold inside an American convenience store. Almost a third of the shop in one category. By 2024, that was down to 18.8%. 8% and the margin is thin around 13.8% gross before a single cost is applied. Compare that with the other tobacco pouches, smokeless, the newer things in little tins. Those run near 29 12%. So the oldest category is shrinking. The thing replacing it is smaller and worth more per sale. That is why 19% of the sales makes 7% of the profit. It is an enormous amount of money moving through a very narrow gap. There is also a reason cigarettes sit behind the counter that has nothing to do with the law. They are reasons to walk in. Whatever else happens on that trip happens because somebody came through the door for a thing they were buying anyway, which is the model. And it is time to say it plainly. Look at what earns and what does not. A gallon of fuel is priced to the scent on a sign facing the road. You can compare it from the driving seat, so it earns almost nothing. A pack of cigarette is a known brand at a known size. You have bought it 100 times. You would notice a change, so it earns almost nothing. A coffee at 10 6 in the morning has no comparison price. There is nothing to compare it to. There is no other coffee. Not here. Not now. That is the business. Everything you could have planned for is cheap. Everything you could not is not. The story is not selling you goods. It is selling you the absence of an alternative. And it prices that by how badly you need one. Which brings us to the cup. In 2005, food and drink prepared in stores was 11.9% of indoor sales. a coffee pot and some rolling hot dogs. Last year it was 28.5%. More to the point, it produced 38.9% of the gross profit made inside the shop. Under 30% of the sales, nearly 40% of the profit, the exact inverse of the fuel. You can see it clean in the accounts of a company that files them. Casey's runs nearly 3,000 across stores in the American Midwest. Last financial year, Casey's made a gross margin of 58.6% on prepared food and dispensed drinks. On packaged groceries and general merchandise, 35.8%. On fuel, around 42 cents a gallon. Put into dollars and the shape of the company appears. Casey's made about $2.7 billion of gross profit inside it shops. On fuel, it's made about 1.5 billion. The pumps are out front. The business is at the back. Casey's sells enough pizza to sit among the larger pizza chains in America. That is not a novelty fact. That is what the company is. A pizza has no shelf price you have memorized. It cannot be bought cheaper 11 miles away because in 11 miles you will not want it. It is made on site so nobody can undercut it on the same forcourt. It is the most protected object in the building, which is why the industry has spent 20 years turning fuel stations into kitchens. The cup has a twin, and it is the largest thing in the shop that nobody talks about, packaged drinks. The cold vault along the back wall. They are now around 18.7% of indoor sales. That makes them the second biggest category in the store. Somewhere in the middle of last year, drinks overtook cigarettes as the leading driver of instore merchandise sales. 50 years of tobacco at the top, beaten by a fridge full of bottles. The logic is the coffeey's logic. A cold drink is bought because it is cold and because it is cold now. The identical bottle warm costs a fraction of that in a supermarket 4 minutes down the road. Nobody buys a warm one here. The refrigeration is the product. The liquid is incidental. And the shelf keeps rearranging itself around whatever people cannot plan for. Snacks sold on protein grew almost 8% last year. Part of that is weight loss drugs. People eating far less are choosing differently in the 10 seconds they spend at that rack. The store has no opinion about any of it. It moves the highest margin thing to eye level and waits. Now, the cost that eats all of it. Last year, the American convenience industry paid $21.3 billion in card processing fees. One year, one industry. 82% of its sales are now paid for by card. The trade body's own position is blunt. Card fees are the second highest operating cost the industry carries. Only wages are bigger. And inside that figure is a detail which is almost funny. A large part of the price of the fuel is tax. The retailer collects it and hands it over. He does not keep a scent of it, but the customer pays the whole amount on card, so the fee is charged on the tax as well. The industry paid roughly $4.6 billion last year in card fees on money that was never its own. The shop on the corner does not set the price of fuel. That is decided upstream. It does not set the price of cigarettes. That is the manufacturer and the tax code. And it does not set the cost of being paid. Three of its largest numbers belong to somebody else. That is the honest reason the coffee costs what it costs. It is the one line on the receipt the owner gets to write. There is one more thing on the counter and it is not a product either. Lottery tickets typically pay the retailer 5 to 7%. On a $5 scratch card, that is a quarter or so. Nobody stays open on a quarter. The lottery is not there to make money. It is there because a lottery player visits far more often than somebody who does not play and almost nobody buys only the ticket. It is a machine for generating visits. It sits beside a wall of things with real margins on them. Same job as the cigarettes. Get the person through the door and let the door do the rest. There is a version of this business that breaks the rule completely and it is where the money is going. A normal American convenience store is small. The traditional format runs about 2 and a half thousand square ft. The trade body defines the whole category as usually under 5,000. By's largest store is 75,593 ft. That is 30 ordinary shops in one building. One of its Texas store has 120 fuel pumps. It has won an award for the best public toilets in America. It runs a car wash with a 250 ft conveyor, which is the longest one on Earth. And it does not want lorry drivers. There is no parking for an 18-wheeler. The one customer a traditional truck stop is built around is the customer this format turns away. Now look at what that does to everything I have just said. The whole model runs on the absence of an alternative. You stop because you have to. You pay because there is nowhere else. Nobody has to stop at Bies. People drive past three other stations to reach one. They plan the journey around it. They queue to get in. There are people who photograph the sign. Convenience is not the product anymore. The store became the destination. And once it is the destination, the pricing logic turns over. You are no longer paying a premium for having a choice. You are paying because you choose. The company has been doing this since 1982 out of Texas. For most of that time, nobody outside Texas has heard of it. Wawa is running the same play in a smaller building. Its chief executive has said food and drink is now more than half the company's revenue. That is not a shop with a kitchen in it. That is a restaurant that happens to sell fuel outside and there is a reason the whole industry is drifting that way. It is not a fashion. The fuel is going to sell less. The trade body's own research director has put the question to members directly. What can you do inside the shop so that as fuel demand declines, you can diversify your revenue and your profit? That is the industry's own association telling its own members to plan for the pumps mattering less. And here is why they can be calm about it. Go back to the first number in this video. Fuel is 65% of the sales and 38.8% of the profit. A business that made most of its money on fuel would be in real trouble. This one does not. The fourcourt was never the business. It was the reason to put a building on that particular piece of ground. The building is the thing that earns. So the plan is a kitchen, a cold vault, and a car wash sold by subscription on a site with parking beside a road. The pumps can stay or go. It barely moves the account. Now the other side, because there is one, it would be easy to stop there and call the whole thing a racket. It is not that simple. Start with who owns these places. There are roughly 152,000 convenience stores in America. About 95,000 of them belong to somebody running 10 locations or fewer. That is not a corporation. That is a family with a shop and a loan. The average store runs about 20 staff on an average wage of just over $15 an hour. Somebody is there at 3:00 in the morning. Somebody cleans the machine, mops the floor, and takes the abuse at closing time. Part of the premium is buying exactly that. A shop that is open when nothing else is has to be staffed when nothing else is. Those are the least pleasant hours in retail. The margins at the bottom are not extravagant either. This is a high volume, low percentage business. The operating costs move faster than the prices do and it is not a safe business to be in. The number of convenience stores in America fell last year. 280 of them went on net after 2 years of the count going up. The ones closing are not the 75,000 ft ones. But one criticism survives all of that. And it is about who pays it. The convenience premium is a charge for not being able to plan ahead. And the people least able to plan ahead are the people with the least money, the least storage, no car to drive to a supermarket with. If you can buy in bulk, you never pay it. If you cannot, you pay it every day on milk, on bread, on ordinary things at prices set for emergencies. That is not a fraud. Nobody is lying about the price. But the cost of being poor ends up built into a bottle of milk. That is worth saying out loud rather than filling it under convenience. So, back to the two answers. Fuel and cigarettes, 65% of the sales, 19% off the shelf, and between them a fraction of the money. They were never the product. They're the reason you stopped. The product is the 90 seconds after you walk in. You are hungry. You are in a hurry. There is nowhere else. and something on that shelf costs whatever they decided it costs. segments.text: The trade body's own research director has put the question to members directly.
segments.viText: Giám đốc nghiên cứu riêng của cơ quan thương mại đã trực tiếp đặt câu hỏi cho các thành viên.

segments.text: What can you do inside the shop so that as fuel demand declines, you can diversify your revenue and your profit?
segments.viText: Bạn có thể làm gì bên trong cửa hàng để khi nhu cầu nhiên liệu giảm, bạn có thể đa dạng hóa doanh thu và lợi nhuận của mình?

segments.text: That is the industry's own association telling its own members to plan for the pumps mattering less.
segments.viText: Đó là hiệp hội của chính ngành đang yêu cầu các thành viên của mình lập kế hoạch cho máy bơm ít quan trọng hơn.

segments.text: And here is why they can be calm about it.
segments.viText: Và đây là lý do tại sao họ có thể bình tĩnh về điều đó.

segments.text: Go back to the first number in this video.
segments.viText: Quay lại số đầu tiên trong video này.

segments.text: Fuel is 65% of the sales and 38.8% of the profit.
segments.viText: Nhiên liệu chiếm 65% doanh thu và 38,8% lợi nhuận.

segments.text: A business that made most of its money on fuel would be in real trouble.
segments.viText: Một doanh nghiệp kiếm được phần lớn tiền từ nhiên liệu sẽ gặp rắc rối thực sự.

segments.text: This one does not.
segments.viText: Cái này thì không.

segments.text: The fourcourt was never the business.
segments.viText: Fourcourt chưa bao giờ là công việc kinh doanh.

segments.text: It was the reason to put a building on that particular piece of ground.
segments.viText: Đó là lý do để xây dựng một tòa nhà trên mảnh đất đặc biệt đó.

segments.text: The building is the thing that earns.
segments.viText: Tòa nhà là thứ kiếm được.

segments.text: So the plan is a kitchen, a cold vault, and a car wash sold by subscription on a site with parking beside a road.
segments.viText: Vì vậy, kế hoạch là một nhà bếp, một kho lạnh và một tiệm rửa xe được bán theo hình thức đăng ký trên một địa điểm có bãi đậu xe bên đường.

segments.text: The pumps can stay or go.
segments.viText: Máy bơm có thể ở lại hoặc đi.

segments.text: It barely moves the account.
segments.viText: Nó hầu như không di chuyển tài khoản.

segments.text: Now the other side, because there is one, it would be easy to stop there and call the whole thing a racket.
segments.viText: Bây giờ là phía bên kia, vì có một cái nên sẽ dễ dàng dừng lại ở đó và gọi toàn bộ sự việc là một cái vợt.

segments.text: It is not that simple.
segments.viText: Nó không đơn giản như vậy.

segments.text: Start with who owns these places.
segments.viText: Bắt đầu với người sở hữu những địa điểm này.

segments.text: There are roughly 152,000 convenience stores in America.
segments.viText: Có khoảng 152.000 cửa hàng tiện lợi ở Mỹ.

segments.text: About 95,000 of them belong to somebody running 10 locations or fewer.
segments.viText: Khoảng 95.000 trong số đó thuộc về ai đó đang điều hành 10 địa điểm hoặc ít hơn.

segments.text: That is not a corporation.
segments.viText: Đó không phải là một tập đoàn.

segments.text: That is a family with a shop and a loan.
segments.viText: Đó là một gia đình có cửa hàng và một khoản vay.

segments.text: The average store runs about 20 staff on an average wage of just over $15 an hour.
segments.viText: Một cửa hàng trung bình có khoảng 20 nhân viên với mức lương trung bình chỉ hơn 15 USD một giờ.

segments.text: Somebody is there at 3:00 in the morning.
segments.viText: Có người ở đó lúc 3 giờ sáng.

segments.text: Somebody cleans the machine, mops the floor, and takes the abuse at closing time.
segments.viText: Ai đó lau máy, lau sàn và lạm dụng lúc đóng cửa.

segments.text: Part of the premium is buying exactly that.
segments.viText: Một phần của phí bảo hiểm là mua chính xác thứ đó.

segments.text: A shop that is open when nothing else is has to be staffed when nothing else is.
segments.viText: Một cửa hàng mở cửa khi không có gì khác thì phải có nhân viên khi không có gì khác.

segments.text: Those are the least pleasant hours in retail.
segments.viText: Đó là những giờ ít dễ chịu nhất trong lĩnh vực bán lẻ.

segments.text: The margins at the bottom are not extravagant either.
segments.viText: Phần lề ở phía dưới cũng không hề xa hoa.

segments.text: This is a high volume, low percentage business.
segments.viText: Đây là một doanh nghiệp có khối lượng lớn, tỷ lệ phần trăm thấp.

segments.text: The operating costs move faster than the prices do and it is not a safe business to be in.
segments.viText: Chi phí vận hành tăng nhanh hơn giá cả và đây không phải là một hoạt động kinh doanh an toàn.

segments.text: The number of convenience stores in America fell last year.
segments.viText: Số lượng cửa hàng tiện lợi ở Mỹ đã giảm trong năm ngoái.

segments.text: 280 of them went on net after 2 years of the count going up.
segments.viText: 280 trong số đó đã vào lưới sau 2 năm tăng lên.

segments.text: The ones closing are not the 75,000 ft ones.
segments.viText: Những cái đóng không phải là những cái ở độ cao 75.000 ft.

segments.text: But one criticism survives all of that.
segments.viText: Nhưng một lời chỉ trích vẫn tồn tại tất cả những điều đó.

segments.text: And it is about who pays it.
segments.viText: Và vấn đề là ai trả tiền.

segments.text: The convenience premium is a charge for not being able to plan ahead.
segments.viText: Phí tiện lợi là một khoản phí cho việc không thể lập kế hoạch trước.

segments.text: And the people least able to plan ahead are the people with the least money, the least storage, no car to drive to a supermarket with.
segments.viText: Và những người ít có khả năng lập kế hoạch trước nhất là những người có ít tiền nhất, ít đồ dự trữ nhất, không có ô tô để lái đến siêu thị.

segments.text: If you can buy in bulk, you never pay it.
segments.viText: Nếu bạn có thể mua với số lượng lớn, bạn sẽ không bao giờ phải trả tiền.

segments.text: If you cannot, you pay it every day on milk, on bread, on ordinary things at prices set for emergencies.
segments.viText: Nếu không thể, bạn phải trả nó hàng ngày bằng sữa, bánh mì, những thứ thông thường với mức giá ấn định cho những trường hợp khẩn cấp.

segments.text: That is not a fraud.
segments.viText: Đó không phải là một sự lừa đảo.

segments.text: Nobody is lying about the price.
segments.viText: Không ai nói dối về giá cả.

segments.text: But the cost of being poor ends up built into a bottle of milk.
segments.viText: Nhưng cái giá của sự nghèo khó cuối cùng lại được tích vào một chai sữa.

segments.text: That is worth saying out loud rather than filling it under convenience.
segments.viText: Điều đó đáng để nói to hơn là lấp đầy nó một cách thuận tiện.

segments.text: So, back to the two answers.
segments.viText: Vì vậy, quay lại với hai câu trả lời.

segments.text: Fuel and cigarettes, 65% of the sales, 19% off the shelf, and between them a fraction of the money.
segments.viText: Nhiên liệu và thuốc lá, 65% doanh số bán hàng, 19% giảm giá và giữa chúng là một phần tiền.

segments.text: They were never the product.
segments.viText: Chúng chưa bao giờ là sản phẩm.

segments.text: They're the reason you stopped.
segments.viText: Họ là lý do bạn dừng lại.

segments.text: The product is the 90 seconds after you walk in.
segments.viText: Sản phẩm sẽ có sau 90 giây kể từ khi bạn bước vào.

segments.text: You are hungry.
segments.viText: Bạn đang đói.

segments.text: You are in a hurry.
segments.viText: Bạn đang vội.

segments.text: There is nowhere else.
segments.viText: Không có nơi nào khác.

segments.text: and something on that shelf costs whatever they decided it costs.
segments.viText: và thứ gì đó trên kệ đó có giá tùy theo quyết định của họ.

segments.text: If you enjoyed this video, make sure to like and subscribe.
segments.viText: Nếu bạn thích video này, hãy nhớ thích và đăng ký.

segments.text: Tony will be posting again in the near future.
segments.viText: Tony sẽ đăng lại trong thời gian tới.

segments.text: Bye-bye.
segments.viText: Tạm biệt.

segments.text: I am waiting.
segments.viText: Tôi đang chờ đợi.
